title: Everyone Said Head Gasket
complaintTemplate: CUST STATES: runs hot on the highway and needs a splash of coolant every week or so. Temp gauge spikes then drops; heater blows cold sometimes. Another shop said head gasket and quoted $2,400 — customer wants a second opinion before spending it.

faultSeeds.internalNote: The expensive answer is the RIGHT one this time — but only provable with a combustion/block test. Combustion gases are entering the coolant (positive block test), pressurizing the system and pushing coolant out; it holds pressure externally. Correct fix: head gasket. Condemning it WITHOUT the block test is a lucky guess, not a diagnosis. Confirming test: act_combustion_test.

activeFaults.label: head gasket leaking combustion gases into the cooling system

resultOverrides.act_combustion_test: The block-test fluid turns yellow within a minute of running — combustion gases are present in the coolant.
resultOverrides.act_pressure_test: It holds 15 psi externally — no drips at the outlet housing or hoses — but the needle creeps up as combustion gas pressurizes the system.
resultOverrides.act_cap_test: The surge-tank cap holds its 15-psi rating on the tester — the cap is fine.
resultOverrides.act_bleed_check: It bleeds and burps, the thermostat opens — then the reservoir pressurizes and pushes over again on the test drive.
resultOverrides.act_top_off: You top it off. Normal in the bay, then the reservoir pressurizes and pushes coolant out within a few heat cycles.

faultSeeds.internalNote: The notorious Cruze 1.4T external leak: the plastic coolant/water-outlet housing at the back of the head cracks at the seam and weeps under pressure. No combustion gases; the system won't hold pressure and you find the source. Correct fix: coolant outlet housing. Condemning the head gasket here is a $2,400 mistake. Confirming test: act_pressure_test.

activeFaults.label: cracked plastic coolant/water-outlet housing weeping under pressure

resultOverrides.act_combustion_test: The block-test fluid stays blue after several minutes running — no combustion gases in the coolant.
resultOverrides.act_pressure_test: It won't hold — pressure bleeds down from 15 psi and coolant weeps from the seam of the plastic coolant/water-outlet housing at the back of the head.
resultOverrides.act_cap_test: The cap holds its 15-psi rating on the tester — not the cap.
resultOverrides.act_bleed_check: It bleeds fine and the thermostat opens, but coolant keeps disappearing between drives.
resultOverrides.act_top_off: You top it off; a damp trail and dried coolant crust show up at the outlet housing by the next morning.

faultSeeds.internalNote: The cheapest fix and the classic Cruze 1.4T trap: a $20 surge-tank pressure cap that won't hold its 15-psi rating, so the system boils up into the reservoir and pushes over. No combustion gases, holds pressure with a tester on, no external leak — the cap itself is the fault. Correct fix: surge-tank cap. Condemning the head gasket here is the worst-value mistake. Confirming test: act_cap_test.

activeFaults.label: surge-tank pressure cap not holding its 15-psi rating

resultOverrides.act_combustion_test: The block-test fluid stays blue — no combustion gases in the coolant.
resultOverrides.act_pressure_test: With the tester's adapter on, the system holds 15 psi steadily — no external leak, no bleed-down.
resultOverrides.act_cap_test: The surge-tank cap won't hold its rating — it vents off well below 15 psi on the tester. It's been releasing early and letting the system boil up into the tank.
resultOverrides.act_bleed_check: It bleeds and burps fine; the thermostat opens. But it still pushes coolant over on a hard heat cycle.
resultOverrides.act_top_off: You top it off; it boils up into the reservoir and pushes over again the next time it gets hot.

faultSeeds.internalNote: No parts. A prior shop did a coolant service and never properly bled this hard-to-fill system — trapped air causes hot spots, gauge spikes, and the cold-heater complaint. No combustion gases, holds pressure, cap holds, no external leak. Correct fix: proper vacuum-fill / bleed, NO PARTS. Condemning the head gasket here is a $2,400 mistake over air. Confirming test: act_bleed_check.

activeFaults.label: trapped air from an improper coolant fill (never correctly bled)

resultOverrides.act_combustion_test: The block-test fluid stays blue — no combustion gases in the coolant.
resultOverrides.act_pressure_test: It holds 15 psi steadily — no external leak, and the cap holds spec.
resultOverrides.act_cap_test: The cap holds its 15-psi rating fine.
resultOverrides.act_bleed_check: As you vacuum-fill it, a big slug of trapped air pulls out of the heater core and block; the upper hose finally heats evenly and the gauge steadies. The last coolant service was never properly bled.
resultOverrides.act_top_off: You top it off; the gauge still spikes on the drive because the air is still trapped.

nodes.prompt: A $2,400 head-gasket quote from the last shop, coolant disappearing weekly, a gauge that spikes and drops. Before you sell — or rule out — that job, where do you start?

options.label: Block/combustion-test the coolant to rule a head gasket in or out
Pressure-test the system and cap, and find where it's going
Pull it in and run a full cooling-system workup
The other shop already said head gasket — just do the job

nodes.prompt: On the lift, cold, cap off. What's your move?

options.label: Block/combustion-test the coolant (combustion gases present?)
Pressure-test the cooling system and look for an external leak
Pressure-test the surge-tank cap on the cap tester
Vacuum-fill / bleed and check for trapped air
Top off the coolant and tell them to watch it
I'm ready to commit to a root cause

nodes.prompt: Combustion gases collect at the highest point of the cooling system. On this car — which is filled at the surge tank, with no radiator cap — where do you draw the block-test sample?
nodes.explanation: The reagent samples vapor at the highest point of the system; this platform fills at the surge tank, so that's where you pull from — there's no radiator cap to sample.

options.label: From the radiator's own cap opening
From the surge-tank neck, engine warm, cap off
From the lower radiator hose down at the pump
From the overflow tube where it vents

nodes.prompt: The block test (combustion-leak test) works by —
nodes.explanation: The blue reagent is pH-sensitive; dissolved combustion CO2 turns it yellow-green. It reacts to combustion-gas chemistry, not to heat or pressure.

options.label: reacting to coolant temperature crossing a set point
trapping hydrocarbons from burning oil in the coolant
changing color as dissolved combustion CO2 shifts its pH
detecting pressure pulses that push vapor up the tube

nodes.prompt: You run the block test — combustion-leak fluid over the surge-tank neck with the engine running — watching for the reagent to change color.

options.label: Log it and cross-check the external side with a pressure test
Log it and commit

nodes.prompt: How do you run the cooling-system pressure test here?
nodes.explanation: You pressurize to the cap's rating cold with a hand pump and watch for bleed-down. Revving the engine or feeding shop air can damage the system or mask where it's actually leaking.

options.label: Pump to the cap's 15-psi rating cold and watch for bleed-down
Rev the engine to build pressure and watch the gauge climb
Feed shop air into the reservoir until it starts to leak
Take it straight to 30 psi to force a hidden leak open

nodes.prompt: You hand-pump the cooling system to 15 psi cold and watch for bleed-down and external seepage.

options.label: Log it and block-test for combustion gases too
Log it and pressure-test the cap on the tester
Log it and commit

nodes.prompt: You put the surge-tank cap on the cap tester and pump it to its rating, watching whether it holds.

options.label: Log it and commit
Cross-check the rest of the system first

nodes.prompt: You vacuum-fill and bleed the system, watching whether the upper hose heats evenly, the thermostat opens, and how much air comes out.

options.label: Log it and commit
Cross-check with a block and pressure test first

nodes.prompt: You top off the coolant.
nodes.continueLabel: That's not a diagnosis — back to the workup.

nodes.prompt: Commit to a specific root cause. Remember the customer is about to spend $2,400 on someone's word.

options.label: It's the head gasket — pull it and do the gasket job
It's the plastic coolant/water-outlet housing — replace it
It's the surge-tank pressure cap — replace the cap
No parts — it was never properly bled; vacuum-fill and burp it
The other shop's probably right — just do the head gasket
Top it off and tell them to keep an eye on it

nodes.prompt: You do the head-gasket job — pull the head, replace the gasket, resurface as needed, refill and bleed. (Book job: ~8 hours, $2,400.)
You replace the plastic coolant/water-outlet housing (and the recovery-tank hose while you're in there), then refill and bleed.
You install a new surge-tank pressure cap — a $20 part, ten minutes.
You properly vacuum-fill and bleed the system — no parts.
You top it off and send it with a 'keep an eye on the level.'
Before you hand back the keys — how do you confirm the fix held?

options.label: Road-test through a full heat cycle and re-run the confirming test
It settled down at idle in the bay — release it

nodes.prompt: You heat-cycle it on a road test and re-run the test that flagged the fault, watching the gauge and the reservoir the whole way.

It holds temperature through a full heat-cycle and road test, no coolant loss, heater hot. Fixed — and if it was the head gasket, you sold it on a positive block test, not a hunch. If it wasn't, you saved the customer $2,400.
It's back, still running hot and dropping coolant. The real cause was never addressed.
